content.text: When FCM or APNs answers your server, the message has been accepted, not delivered. The device and the OS then decide when it arrives, and sometimes whether it arrives at all: pushes get delayed, collapsed, reordered and expired. Use a push to show the user something or to hint that data changed, and let the app fetch the real state from your server.

A clinic booking app moves an appointment from 4 pm to 2 pm. The server sends a data message with the new time, the app writes it into its local list of appointments, and the server marks the patient as notified. The next day support gets a complaint: the patient came at 4 pm, and the app still says 4 pm. The server logs show that FCM returned a message ID. Nobody can say what happened after that, because nothing in the design ever checked.
The common misconception
The belief: once FCM or APNs accepts a push, the phone receives it, the app runs, and the local data is updated. So the server can push the new state and move on, with no polling and no sync.

It's an easy belief to hold. In development the phone sits on your desk, plugged in, with the app open a minute ago, and every push arrives within a second. The send API returns a message ID that looks like a receipt. The word "push" itself suggests the server is in control. And most of the time, messages do arrive quickly. That's the half-truth: delivery is usually fast, but it isn't promised, and the failures land on the devices you rarely test: idle, offline, saving battery, or with the app swiped away.
What actually happens
A message ID means "accepted", not "delivered"

Firebase's docs are direct about this: when your server "receives a message ID back, it doesn't mean that the message was already delivered to the device. Instead, it means that it was accepted for delivery." If the device isn't connected, FCM stores the message until it is. By default a message lives for four weeks, and you can set its
ttl
anywhere from 0 to 2,419,200 seconds (28 days). A
ttl

of 0 means a message that can't be delivered immediately is discarded. And on Android, if a device hasn't connected to FCM for more than a month, FCM "still accepts the message but immediately discards it."
Apple calls APNs "a best-effort service". If it can't deliver right away, it may store the notification for up to 30 days, depending on the
apns-expiration
you set, and it warns that notifications "may also get throttled, saved in storage, and in some cases, not delivered."
The OS decides when your app hears about it
On Android, normal priority is the default for both data and notification messages. Normal messages arrive right away when the device is awake, but in
Doze mode

"delivery may be delayed to conserve battery until the device exits doze." High priority can wake a sleeping device, but it's reserved for messages that show the user something: if FCM "detects a pattern in which messages don't result in user-facing notifications, your messages may be deprioritized to normal priority". FCM's newer
AndroidConfigV2
API, still in preview, makes the split explicit:
RemoteNotification
for urgent, visible notifications and
BackgroundSync
for updates whose delivery "can be batched or delayed".
On iOS, a background notification (
content-available
with
apns-priority

5) is the tool for silent updates, and Apple's docs say the system "doesn't guarantee their delivery". They advise sending no more than two or three per hour. The system may hold one back; when a newer one arrives, it keeps only the newest, and "if something force quits or kills the app, the system discards the held notification." And when a push does wake the app, the work must be quick: iOS gives it 30 seconds, and FCM's Android docs say the time in
onMessageReceived
is "only expected to be long enough to immediately render a notification". A backgrounded app can be stopped at any moment, as the article on the app lifecycle and process death explains.
Messages get collapsed, capped and reordered
A
collapsible message

replaces an older one with the same collapse key that's still waiting. That's what you want for "sync now", but it means the device never sees the older payload. APNs goes further: when it can't deliver right away, it stores "only one notification per bundle ID".
Non-collapsible messages are capped. On Android, FCM stores at most 100 of them for a device; past that, "all stored messages are discarded," and the app later gets a special message (
onDeletedMessages
in the Android SDK) that is its cue to do a full sync.

Order isn't promised either. FCM "doesn't guarantee the order of delivery", and APNs "may reorder notifications you send to the same device token." If each push carries a new state, an old state can arrive last and win.
Push as a hint, sync as the truth
The fix is to stop treating the payload as the update. The push says "something changed"; the app asks the server what changed, using a token that remembers where its last sync ended.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: Now a lost push costs a delay, not a wrong screen: the next resume or the next push pulls the same change. Duplicates, collapsed pings and out-of-order arrivals all trigger the same pull, and since applying the same changes twice leaves the same result, the extra pulls are harmless. That's
idempotency
doing the work. A visible notification still carries its own text, "Your appointment moved to 2 pm", which the system can show without running your app.

rows.text: A message ID means the phone got it
It means FCM accepted it for delivery
Every push is stored until delivered
Messages expire, collapse, and on Android are capped at 100 pending
Pushes arrive in the order you send them
Neither FCM nor APNs guarantees order
A data push always wakes the app
Doze delays normal priority; iOS treats background pushes as low priority
Without visible notifications, FCM may deprioritize it

blocks.title: High priority isn't a fix for silent syncs

content.text: FCM looks at seven days of message behavior for each app instance. If high priority messages don't lead to visible notifications, later ones may be lowered to normal priority. The same happens if the user turned off notifications for your app, because none of your notifications can be posted.

blocks.title: Put a version in every push

content.text: Add the record's version or update time to the payload. Before acting on a push, compare it with what the app already has and ignore it if it isn't newer. A late, reordered push then can't move the app backwards.
How to apply it in your project
Search your push handlers for payload fields written to storage or app state. Each one is a place where a missed push leaves the app wrong.

items.title: Give the app a pull path

content.text: Add an endpoint that returns changes since a token, and call it on app start, on resume, on every push and when the app learns that stored messages were deleted.

items.title: Pick the message by its job

content.text: Visible, urgent messages get a notification payload and high priority (
apns-priority
10 on iOS). Background refreshes get normal priority or a background notification, a collapse key, and a
ttl
that matches how long they're useful.
Don't mark a user as informed when the send succeeds. If something must reach them, show it in the app on the next sync as well, or use a channel you can confirm.
Put an Android device into Doze, swipe the app away on iOS, disable notifications, and check that the app still ends up showing the right data.
Key takeaways

items.text: A message ID from FCM means the message was accepted, not delivered.
Doze, priority rules, TTL, collapsing and reordering all sit between your server and your app.
On iOS, background pushes are low priority, rate-limited and dropped when the app is force quit.
Use the push as a hint and keep the truth on the server, synced on start, resume and push.
Make syncing idempotent, so duplicate, late or out-of-order pushes are harmless.
